passages.t: Manasseh, and five daughters who came to claim their share
passages.happening:
The lot for Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn, is described next. One part of the tribe, the family of Machir, had already received Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan (verse 1). The rest of the clans now receive land west of the river (verse 2).

One man of the tribe, Zelophehad, had died with no sons. “These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah” (verse 3).

The five come before Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the leaders, and say, “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers” (verse 4).

“So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD” (verse 4). Because of their shares, Manasseh receives ten portions west of the Jordan (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
The five sisters have been in the story before. In the book of Numbers, while Israel was still in the wilderness, they came to Moses with a question. In Israel land passed from father to son. Their father had no son. Was his name to disappear from his clan, and were they to have nothing? Moses took the case to God, and God said that the daughters were right. A new law was given: where a man had no sons, his daughters would inherit.

That was a promise about land Israel did not yet have. Now the land is being divided, years later, and the five women come to see that the promise is kept.

Their speech is worth noticing. They do not plead. They do not ask the leaders to be generous. They say what the LORD commanded. They hold the leaders of Israel to God's own word, in public, and the leaders do as he said.

The writer names all five, as Numbers does each time they appear. In a chapter of clan names and borders, their names are kept.

Several of the clan names in this passage have turned up outside the Bible. Pieces of inscribed pottery from the eighth century BC, found at Samaria, record deliveries of oil and wine from districts with these names. Two of the districts are called Hoglah and Noah. The names of two of the sisters became the names of places.

The ruling had limits. It applied only when there were no sons, and a later chapter of Numbers added that the women must marry within their own tribe. It was a real protection in its world and not the last word on the standing of women. But the direction of it is plain. When five women with no standing by custom brought their case, God took their side.
passages.later:
The ruling was given in Numbers: “The daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly. You certainly must give them property as an inheritance among their father’s brothers, and transfer their father’s inheritance to them” (Numbers 27:7).

Paul writes of an inheritance in which the usual lines of standing make no difference: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:28-29).
passages.asks: Five sisters stood before the leaders of the nation and said what God had commanded. Ask whether there is a promise of God you have been too timid to hold on to. Ask whether you believe he has made room for you by name. And if you have the power to give or withhold what belongs to someone else, ask whether they would have to fight you for it.

passages.t: Manasseh's border, and the cities it could not take
passages.happening:
The writer traces the line between Manasseh and Ephraim, from near Shechem south to the Brook of Kanah and west to the sea. Ephraim lies to the south and Manasseh to the north, with the tribes of Asher and Issachar beyond (verses 7-10).

Manasseh is also assigned a row of strong cities that stand in the land of those neighbors: Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo, each with the settlements around it (verse 11).

“But the descendants of Manasseh were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land. However, when the Israelites grew stronger, they put the Canaanites to forced labor; but they failed to drive them out completely” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Manasseh's share west of the Jordan took in the northern part of the central hills and reached toward the wide, rich Valley of Jezreel.

The six cities in verse 11 were not ordinary towns. They guarded that valley and the roads through it. Megiddo and Taanach stood over the passes. Beth-shean had been a center of Egyptian rule in the region. They were the strongest places in the north, set on open ground.

These were exactly the cities Manasseh could not take. The writer says so in a plain sentence and gives a plain reason. The people who lived there were determined to stay.

This is the third chapter in a row to end a tribe's account with an admission. Judah could not drive out the people of Jerusalem. Ephraim did not drive out the people of Gezer. Manasseh could not occupy the cities of the valley. The pattern is deliberate. The writer is preparing the reader for the book of Judges.

The second sentence repeats what Ephraim did at Gezer. When Israel grew strong enough to remove these peoples, it chose to use them. The note on chapter 16 says why that was a failure in the book's own terms and a wrong in itself.
passages.later:
Judges opens with this very list: “At that time Manasseh failed to drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo, and their villages; for the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land” (Judges 1:27).

Then it gives God's verdict on the whole unfinished state of things: “Yet you have not obeyed My voice. What is this you have done?” (Judges 2:2).
passages.asks: The writer set down Manasseh's failure in one honest sentence. Ask what you would write if you had to put your own unfinished obedience into one line. Then look at the second sentence. When Israel grew stronger it used its strength for its own gain. Ask what you have done with the strength, money or standing you have gained since you were weak.

passages.happening:
The people of Joseph come to Joshua with a complaint. “Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance? We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly” (verse 14).

Joshua gives them their own argument back. If they are so many, they can go up into the forest and clear land for themselves (verse 15).

They answer that the hills are not enough, and that the Canaanites in the valleys ‘have iron chariots’ (verse 16).

Joshua does not give way. “You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment, because the hill country will be yours as well. It is a forest; clear it, and its farthest limits will be yours. Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
Joshua himself was of the tribe of Ephraim. The people complaining to him are his own kin, and they may have hoped for a favor. They do not get one.

Their complaint sounds devout. They say that the LORD has made them many. But what they want is more land handed to them, and what they have not done is use the land they were given. Much of the central hill country was still covered with forest. Turning a wooded hillside into terraced fields was slow, heavy work. And the open valleys below were held by people with the best weapons of the age.

Iron chariots were probably chariots strengthened or fitted with iron. On flat ground they were frightening. In wooded hills they were close to useless. That is one reason Israel settled the highlands first.

Joshua does not deny any of this. He does not say the forest is small or the chariots weak. He says, ‘although they are strong, you can drive them out’. He takes the two things the people have said about themselves, that they are many and that God has prospered them, and tells them that these are reasons to work and not reasons to be given more.

His answer names two kinds of faithfulness. One is with an axe, clearing ground no one else wants. The other is against chariots, facing what frightens them. The people had asked for neither.

The settlement of the hills was done tree by tree.
passages.later:
The book of Judges records that the chariots went on being a reason: Judah ‘could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron’ (Judges 1:19).

Joshua took no large share for himself. When the land was all divided, he asked for one town in the hills of Ephraim: “He rebuilt the city and settled in it” (Joshua 19:50).
passages.hard:
If God was with Israel, why could the tribes not drive out the people with iron chariots?

Verse 12 says Manasseh was unable to take the valley cities. Some readers take that as a simple military report. The hill tribes did not have the weapons to fight on the plains.

The book adds something to that. Joshua says in verse 18 that Joseph can drive the Canaanites out in spite of the chariots. And the book of Judges, looking back, puts the unfinished conquest down to Israel's own disobedience (Judges 2:1-3). On this reading the failure does not show a limit to God's power. It shows Israel's fear, and its unwillingness to trust him in the open country.

Other readers add that the book is frank about the distance between what was promised and what was possessed, and they count that frankness as a mark of its honesty.

The verse is about ancient Israel and a task God had given it. It is not a rule that anyone who fails at something lacked faith. The Bible refuses that reasoning when it is used against people who suffer.
passages.asks: The people of Joseph wanted more given to them and had not cleared what they had. Ask what ‘forest’ lies inside the share God has already given you: the unused gift, the neglected relationship, the hard ground no one else wants. Ask what ‘iron chariots’ you keep naming as the reason you cannot go further. And ask whether your complaint to God is dressed, as theirs was, in the language of thanks.
